items.title: L14: Urgent requests that collide with need to know
items.source: Government Security Classifications Policy; Government Functional Standard for Security, GOV.UK
items.body: Few security decisions are harder than the urgent request from someone senior. A director wants a paper from a restricted team by the end of the day. A minister's office asks for a briefing that mixes material from several sources. A colleague in another department says a decision cannot wait. Need to know and clearance do not disappear because a request is urgent or comes from a senior person. Seniority does not create need to know, although a senior person may well have it. Your task is to separate the real need from the pressure. Start by asking what exactly is wanted and what it will be used for. Often the purpose can be met by a summary at a lower classification, a verbal briefing to cleared people, or a redacted extract. Check that the requester holds the clearance for the material and a genuine business reason; if you cannot confirm it, ask the information owner, who is the person or team responsible for the material and decides who may see it. Do not send material by an unapproved route because the approved one is slow; use secure channels and, if the approved route truly cannot meet the deadline, escalate the delivery problem, not the risk. Keep a note of what was shared, with whom and on whose authority. Where the request is from someone you cannot easily challenge, remember that a polite and professional question is normally welcomed by those who understand security, and the senior person may be the one most exposed if a mistake happens. A manager who models this behaviour shows the team that it is safe to ask. If someone insists that rules be bypassed, treat that as a reportable concern, not a debate you must win on your own.

questions.prompt: A director asks you for a restricted team's paper by the end of the day, and you cannot confirm that the director has a need to know. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send the paper, because a director's seniority is enough to establish a need to know
Send an edited version without telling the director that parts of it were removed
Tell the director that nobody below the director's grade is allowed to share anything restricted
Ask the information owner whether the director may see it, and meanwhile offer a summary that can safely be shared

questions.hint: The information owner decides who may see the material.

questions.prompt: Which statement about seniority and need to know is most accurate?

options.text: Seniority removes the need for any further check on whether the person should see the material
Seniority creates a need to know only for material at OFFICIAL
Seniority does not create a need to know, though a senior person may well have one
Seniority matters only where the requester is a minister

questions.hint: Need to know rests on role and purpose, not rank.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to ask what a requester will use the material for?

options.text: The purpose determines which grade of staff may handle the request
The purpose can often be met by a lower-classified summary, a verbal briefing or a redacted extract
The purpose decides how many copies of the material should be made for the requester
The purpose decides whether the request counts as urgent in law

questions.hint: Understanding purpose can reduce the risk without blocking the work.

questions.prompt: Who is the information owner?

options.text: The person or team responsible for the material, who decides who may see it
Anyone who has previously seen the material and kept a copy
The member of staff who wrote the first draft and so is presumed to own the final text
The head of the department's security team, for every item of information

questions.prompt: The approved secure channel is slow and a deadline is near. What is the right response?

options.text: Use an unapproved route this once, and record it afterwards
Escalate the delivery problem while still using the secure channel
Send the material by personal email to be safe on time
Ask the recipient to collect a printed copy from the printer, without any record of who took it

questions.hint: Escalate the delivery problem, not the risk.

questions.prompt: What should you record after sharing sensitive material in response to an urgent request?

options.text: How quickly the request was dealt with, so that response times can be measured
Who in the team was most helpful in finding the material needed for the request
Whether the requester thanked the team for their help, to inform future handling of requests
What was shared, with whom and on whose authority

questions.prompt: A senior person insists that normal controls should be bypassed 'just this once'. How should the manager treat this?

options.text: As a reportable concern, not a debate to be won alone
As a normal management instruction that overrides the controls
As a reason to refuse all contact with that person in future
As a minor matter to be forgotten once the deadline has passed

questions.hint: Pressure to bypass controls should be reported.

questions.prompt: Why might a polite question about need to know be welcomed even by a senior person?

options.text: Senior people are always more relaxed about security than junior staff
Questions help the senior person to avoid having to hold a clearance at all in the future
Those who understand security know that they, too, are exposed if a mistake happens
Questions are required by law before any senior person is given a document

questions.prompt: A minister's office asks for a briefing that mixes material from several sources. What is a sensible first step?

options.text: Combine the sources and assume the highest classification of any one source applies automatically
Assume that any material in a minister's briefing can be released to the office
Check the classification and ownership of each source and ask the owners where needed
Use the lowest classification among the sources, to make sharing easier

questions.hint: Mixed sources need checking, and aggregation can raise the handling level.

questions.prompt: What does a manager who models the 'ask first' habit achieve?

options.text: It removes the need for any written record of decisions
It shows the team that it is safe to ask questions about security
It makes the manager the sole decision-maker on all access requests
It ensures that no request can ever be refused

items.title: L14: Sharing information across boundaries
items.source: Government Security Classifications Policy; UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018, GOV.UK
items.body: Government work depends on sharing information between teams, departments, arm's-length bodies, local authorities, contractors and international partners. Sharing is not the opposite of security. It is a managed process, and the right question is not whether to share but how, with whom, under what conditions and at what protection. Three questions guide a manager. First, is there a lawful and proper basis? For personal data, data protection law requires a lawful basis, and sharing must be fair, transparent, limited to what is necessary, and secure. Many departments use data sharing agreements that set out the purpose, the data involved, who may access it, how it will be protected, how long it will be held and how problems will be handled. Second, is the recipient authorised and able to protect it? Check clearance, need to know and the recipient's systems. The classification marking tells the recipient how to handle it, so check that it is applied correctly before sending. Third, is the channel suitable? Use approved systems, not personal email, consumer messaging or unapproved cloud tools. Contractors and suppliers who handle government information should be bound by contract and security requirements, and a supplier who handles personal data on the department's behalf is a processor, which needs a written contract setting out its duties. Data sent abroad raises additional requirements, so seek advice before it is shared with international partners. Sharing less is sometimes better: minimise, redact or anonymise where the purpose allows. Finally, keep a record, because a later question about who had access to what must be answerable.

questions.prompt: A team asks whether it can share a dataset with another department. Which question comes first?

options.text: Is there a lawful and proper basis for the sharing, and what is its purpose?
How large the other department's team is, since larger teams are more difficult to trust
Can the data be sent on a personal device to save time on the transfer, just this once?
Has the other department asked for the data before?

questions.hint: Purpose and basis are the starting point.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a data sharing agreement?

options.text: To record that the sharing department has handed over responsibility for the data
To replace the need for any classification marking on the material
To allow either party to use the data for any further purpose it likes
To set out the purpose, the data involved, who may access it, how it is protected, how long it is held and how problems are handled

questions.hint: Agreements fix the terms of sharing.

questions.prompt: What does 'limited to what is necessary' mean for personal data sharing?

options.text: Share all the data available in case it is needed later
Share only the data needed for the stated purpose
Share the data only with people of senior grades
Share the data only once, whatever the purpose

questions.prompt: Why check that the classification marking is correct before sending material?

options.text: The marking tells the recipient how to handle it, so a wrong marking leads to wrong protection
The marking decides how quickly the material must be delivered
The marking decides whether the recipient needs a pass
The marking is used to charge the recipient for the material

questions.prompt: A supplier handles personal data on the department's behalf. What is the supplier called, and what is needed?

options.text: A controller, which needs no contract because it is independent
A recipient, which is bound only by general good manners and by ordinary professional courtesy
A processor, which needs a written contract setting out its duties
A subject, which must be registered with the department

questions.prompt: Which channel is suitable for sharing sensitive government information?

options.text: A personal email account, so long as the message and its attachments are encrypted first
A consumer messaging app, so long as the group is small
A free cloud storage service, so long as the link is private
Approved systems that the department has set up for the purpose

questions.prompt: The department wants to send personal data to an international partner. What should the manager do?

options.text: Send it as normal, since data protection law applies only to transfers inside the United Kingdom
Seek advice, because additional requirements apply to data sent abroad
Remove the names and send it by ordinary email
Ask the partner to pick it up in person

questions.prompt: Which approach reduces risk where the purpose allows?

options.text: Sharing the full dataset with a warning to be careful
Sharing the data with as many parties as possible, so that the risk is spread
Delaying the sharing until the data is out of date
Minimising, redacting or anonymising the data before sharing

questions.prompt: Why keep a record of what was shared and with whom?

options.text: Records are needed to calculate the cost of sharing
Records are required before any data can be deleted
A later question about who had access to what must be answerable
Records allow the department to recover the data from recipients

questions.prompt: A recipient asks to use shared data for a new, different purpose. What should the manager do?

options.text: Treat it as a new request and check the basis and the agreement again
Allow it, because the data has already been shared
Allow it if the recipient is another government department
Refuse any use of the data beyond the first purpose, without discussion

questions.hint: A new purpose needs a new assessment.

items.title: L14: Care and duty when a colleague is in difficulty
items.source: National Security Vetting guidance; Civil Service Code; Equality Act 2010, GOV.UK
items.body: The hardest people-management situations in a security context involve both a duty of care and a duty to protect information, sometimes with legal constraints on what you may do. Imagine a cleared member of your team who is depressed, drinking heavily, or being pressured by a person outside work. Health information is special category data, and in many cases a disability under the Equality Act 2010. You may be told in confidence; you must use the information only for legitimate purposes, tell only those who need to know, and take advice from HR or occupational health before acting on health matters. At the same time you cannot ignore behaviour that affects judgement or security. The balance has several parts. Focus on observable behaviour and its impact, not diagnosis. Offer support and adjustments early, and show the person where help is available. Explain, without threat, that the department has a process for reporting changes in circumstances, and that early honesty is valued. Seek advice from security on whether a report is needed, rather than deciding it for yourself. Do not make assumptions about what a condition means for someone's reliability, because many people with health conditions are entirely reliable. Similarly, a pattern of poor behaviour should not be excused because the person is unwell; it should be addressed fairly and with appropriate adjustments. If you believe there is an immediate risk, such as a threat to the person's safety or to the security of information, act at once and follow emergency procedures.  Agree with the person what will be shared and with whom wherever you can, and explain what you cannot keep confidential. Keep checking in afterwards, because one conversation is rarely enough.

questions.prompt: A cleared team member tells you in confidence that they are struggling with heavy drinking. What is the best approach?

options.text: Keep the information entirely to yourself, since it was told in confidence and cannot be shared at all
Tell the team so that colleagues can keep an eye on the person
Send an email to security with a full account and your own view of the person's reliability
Offer support, take advice from HR or occupational health, and ask security whether a report is needed

questions.hint: Balance care with the duty to seek advice.

questions.prompt: Why is health information handled with particular care?

options.text: It is always classified at SECRET, because information about a person's health is extremely sensitive
It must be reported to the ICO whenever it is recorded
It is special category data and may also relate to a disability under the Equality Act
It can be shared freely among managers, because they all have a legitimate interest in staff wellbeing

questions.hint: Special category data requires stronger protection.

questions.prompt: What should a manager focus on when concerned about a colleague's behaviour?

options.text: Observable behaviour and its impact, not diagnosis
The most likely medical explanation for the behaviour
Rumours from colleagues about the person's private life
The person's character as shown in earlier years

questions.hint: Describe what you see, not what you think it means.

questions.prompt: Why is it unsafe to assume that a health condition makes a person unreliable?

options.text: The Official Secrets Act forbids managers from drawing conclusions about health
Many people with health conditions are entirely reliable, and assumptions may amount to discrimination
Health conditions are never relevant to security in any circumstances, so no judgement is needed
Reliability is judged only by people who are medically qualified

questions.hint: Assumptions can be wrong and unlawful.

questions.prompt: A person's poor behaviour continues, but they have a health condition. How should the manager proceed?

options.text: Excuse it entirely, because the person is unwell and that explains everything the manager has seen
Address the behaviour fairly, with appropriate adjustments and support
Treat it as misconduct without considering the health condition
Wait for the condition to improve before saying anything

questions.hint: Both fairness and support are needed.

questions.prompt: A manager believes there is an immediate threat to a colleague's safety. What is the right action?

options.text: Act at once and follow emergency procedures
Wait until the next one-to-one to raise it
Ask a colleague to talk to the person informally
Record the concern and review it at the end of the week

questions.hint: Immediate risk calls for immediate action.

questions.prompt: Who should know the details of a colleague's health condition?

options.text: The whole team, so that support is consistent and nobody inadvertently makes things worse
Any manager of the same grade, since they share the same responsibilities as the line manager
Security by default, with a copy to the line manager's manager
Only those who need to know, such as HR or occupational health where appropriate

questions.prompt: Why agree with the person what will be shared and with whom, wherever possible?

options.text: It removes any legal responsibility for sharing the information
It means that nothing else needs to be shared
It maintains trust and is more likely to lead to honest engagement
It allows the manager to avoid explaining the limits of confidentiality

questions.prompt: What is the weakness of offering support in only one conversation?

options.text: A single conversation counts as a formal warning
Support that stops after a single conversation is rarely enough, so regular checking in is needed
Repeated support breaches the person's privacy
Support of any kind is the responsibility of HR alone

questions.prompt: What is the danger of excusing poor behaviour because the person is unwell?

options.text: It is always unlawful under the Equality Act to make any allowance for a person's health
It counts as an admission by the manager of discrimination
It removes the person's right to reasonable adjustments, which only apply to those who behave well
It can be unfair to the person and the team, and it can leave a risk unaddressed

items.title: L14: Incidents with unclear ownership and third parties
items.source: Government Functional Standard for Security; supplier security guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: Many incidents do not sit neatly within your team. A supplier tells you that its system, which holds data you supplied, has been compromised. A shared mailbox is used by several teams and one member leaves an attachment on a public link. A colleague from another department mentions that your team's files were visible in a shared folder. A shared account is used by several people and unusual activity appears. Such cases test who owns the incident and who needs to be told. A good approach has four elements. First, report quickly to your own security team, even if you think the incident belongs to someone else. They can work out who owns it. Second, where a third party is involved, contracts normally require a supplier to notify the department promptly of incidents and to cooperate. Do not assume the supplier will handle everything; the department remains responsible for its information and, for personal data, usually remains the controller, who has duties of its own. Third, separate actions: contain, evidence, notify, communicate. Different people may do each, and the manager's job is to make sure none is missed and that nobody duplicates or contradicts the others. Fourth, think about who might be affected: other departments using the same system, individuals whose data is involved, or a wider public. Shared accounts create difficulties because activity cannot be attributed to a single person, which weakens accountability and makes investigation harder; they should generally be avoided or tightly controlled. A situation with several owners needs a single point of coordination, often the security team or the departmental incident lead. Do not wait to be sure whose problem it is. If you are unsure, report anyway, and say what you know and what you do not.

questions.prompt: A supplier tells you its system holding your data has been compromised. What should the manager do first?

options.text: Wait for the supplier to complete its own investigation and report the result
Ask the supplier to delete all the data it holds on the department's behalf
Report it quickly to the department's own security team and follow their lead
Tell the affected team's customers directly before telling anyone in the department

questions.hint: Report internally at once; the department remains responsible.

questions.prompt: Why should the department not assume a supplier will handle an incident entirely?

options.text: The department remains responsible for its information and, for personal data, usually remains the controller with duties of its own
Suppliers are legally forbidden to investigate incidents
Suppliers have no obligation to cooperate with the department
Suppliers can handle only incidents involving classified information

questions.prompt: A colleague from another department tells you your team's files were visible in a shared folder. What should you do?

options.text: Leave it to the colleague's department, since it owns the folder
Wait to see whether anyone has accessed the files before reporting
Move the files quietly to a safer folder without telling anyone about what was found
Report it to your security team promptly, even though the folder belongs to another department

questions.hint: Report even where ownership is unclear.

questions.prompt: Why is a shared account a problem when something goes wrong?

options.text: Shared accounts are always blocked by the system after an incident
Activity cannot be attributed to one person, which weakens accountability and investigation
Shared accounts cannot be used for any work above the classification of OFFICIAL
Shared accounts must be deleted whenever any incident is reported

questions.prompt: Which of these correctly lists separate actions in incident handling?

options.text: Investigate, discipline, publish and close, with each action taken by the same person in turn
Delay, deny, delegate and disclose, with each action handled by the team with the most staff
Contain, preserve evidence, notify and communicate, which may be done by different people
Review, restructure, report and replace, with every action left until the incident has ended

questions.prompt: Several teams own part of an incident. What is usually needed?

options.text: A single point of coordination, often the security team or the incident lead
A separate investigation by each team, so that no team's conclusions influence another's
An agreement that the team with the most staff will take charge
A meeting of all team members to vote on who owns it

questions.prompt: A manager is unsure whose problem an incident is. What is the best course?

options.text: Wait until it is clear whose problem it is, so that nobody reports something that belongs elsewhere
Ask the person who first noticed the incident to decide for themselves whether it should be reported
Report it anyway, saying what is known and what is not
Investigate privately until ownership is clear

questions.hint: Do not wait to settle ownership.

questions.prompt: Why should a manager think about who else might be affected?

options.text: Other departments, individuals whose data is involved or the public may be affected, and may need to be told
Only the manager's own team can ever be affected
Others are affected only if the incident is reported externally
Only people with security clearance can be affected

questions.hint: The reach of an incident may be wider than first thought.

questions.prompt: What do contracts normally require of a supplier in an incident?

options.text: To investigate in secret and report only the outcome
To notify the department promptly and cooperate
To accept all legal liability regardless of cause
To delete all records of the incident

questions.prompt: What should a manager avoid when several people are working on the same incident?

options.text: Writing down what has been done and when, since a record could be used in later review
Reporting progress to security at regular intervals during the incident, as it develops
Reviewing the incident afterwards, once the immediate response has been completed and closed
Duplicating or contradicting each other's actions and messages

items.title: L14: Hard cases in breach assessment
items.source: ICO guidance on personal data breaches; UK GDPR, GOV.UK
items.body: Breach assessment becomes difficult when facts are incomplete or the situation is changing. Specialists will lead, but a manager who understands the harder cases helps them to move quickly. One difficulty is an ongoing breach, for example a misconfigured system which is still exposing data. The priority is to stop the exposure, which may mean switching off the service or a feature, even though that has a cost. A second is uncertainty about numbers or content. The 72-hour limit does not wait for full information: an organisation can notify in phases, giving what it knows and following up as it learns more. A third is children's data and other vulnerable groups, which increases the likelihood that a breach is high-risk. A fourth is special category and criminal offence data. A fifth is where the department is a processor for another organisation, in which case it must tell that organisation without undue delay and follow its instructions. A sixth is where the data was encrypted, but the key may also have been exposed, so assess whether the protection was effective. A seventh is where a recipient is a professional with confidentiality duties, such as a lawyer or another public body, which may reduce risk. An eighth is deciding to tell individuals even where not strictly required, for example to help them protect themselves from fraud. The ICO may ask questions after notification, and records of the reasoning are important. Never alter or backdate records of a breach. Do not make public statements without clearance from the right people. The most common error is delay caused by waiting for certainty. Report what you know, flag what you do not, and update as you learn more.

questions.prompt: A misconfigured system is still exposing data. What is the first priority?

options.text: Calculating exactly how many people are affected
Stopping the exposure, even if this means switching off a service
Writing a full report for the ICO before any step is taken to stop the exposure
Waiting for the next scheduled maintenance window

questions.prompt: The 72-hour limit is approaching but the facts are incomplete. What can the organisation do?

options.text: Wait until all the facts are known, then notify
Withhold notification until the cause is identified
Notify only the individuals affected, and leave the ICO until the facts are fully known
Notify with what is known and follow up as more is learned

questions.prompt: Why does children's data increase concern in an assessment?

options.text: Children are a vulnerable group, so a breach is more likely to be high-risk
Children's data is always classified at TOP SECRET and so any breach would be high-risk
Children's data must be deleted whenever breached
Children's data can be shared freely among departments, which is why a breach is more serious

questions.prompt: A department is a processor for another organisation and finds a breach. What must it do?

options.text: Decide on its own whether the ICO should be told, because it holds the data in its systems
Wait for the other organisation to discover the breach by itself before saying anything
Tell that organisation without undue delay and follow its instructions
Contact affected individuals directly without telling anyone

questions.prompt: Encrypted data was exposed, but the key may also have been exposed. What does this suggest?

options.text: The data is safe, because it was encrypted, and no further assessment of the position is needed
Whether the protection was effective needs to be assessed
The breach does not need to be recorded, since encryption means that no personal data was exposed
The key's exposure is irrelevant, because encryption is a legal defence against any claim

questions.hint: Encryption helps only if the key is secure.

questions.prompt: When might a recipient's duties lower the risk of a breach?

options.text: Where the recipient is a friend of the sender
Where the recipient is unknown but located in the same city
Where the recipient is a professional or public body with confidentiality duties and has confirmed deletion
Where the recipient has said they do not intend to use the data

questions.prompt: Why might a department tell individuals even if not strictly required?

options.text: To reduce the department's costs by avoiding any later claims for compensation
To avoid the need to inform the ICO, since individuals can complain directly instead
To transfer responsibility for protecting the data to the individuals who are affected by it
To help them protect themselves, for example against fraud

questions.prompt: What should never be done with records of a breach?

options.text: Alter or backdate them
Update them as facts emerge
Record the reasoning for decisions
Share them with the specialists

questions.hint: Records must be accurate and honest.

questions.prompt: Why should a manager not make a public statement about a breach on their own?

options.text: Managers are barred from speaking to anyone outside the department
Public statements are always illegal during a breach
Statements need clearance from the right people so that they are accurate and consistent
Public statements about breaches are required by law to be made by the ICO and not the department

questions.prompt: What is the most common error in breach handling?

options.text: Delay caused by waiting for certainty
Reporting too quickly with incomplete information
Recording too much detail
Telling too many specialists

items.title: L14: Conflicts at senior levels
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; Cabinet Office guidance on managing conflicts, GOV.UK
items.body: As responsibilities grow, conflicts of interest become less obvious and carry higher stakes. A senior official may sit on boards, advise on appointments, oversee funding or regulate bodies connected with their own past or family. The principles stay the same, but the practice demands more rigour. A first requirement is a full and honest declaration, kept up to date, covering financial interests, family and close personal connections, past employment, outside roles and anything that others might reasonably think relevant. A second is a decision on management, ideally documented and agreed with someone independent of the person, not self-assessed. A third is the discipline of recusal: if you have an interest in a matter, you do not take part in the discussion or decision, receive papers on it, or influence others informally. A fourth is the risk of the quiet conversation. Hallway chats, private messages and informal hints can circumvent a formal recusal, so the person must stay entirely clear. A fifth is recognition that conflicts can arise from loyalty and gratitude as well as money, for example towards a former employer or a mentor. A sixth is awareness that conflicts can be created by others: a lobbyist may cultivate a relationship that later makes a decision look compromised. A seventh is the responsibility of those who work for senior people. A private office or team member who notices a possible unmanaged conflict should say so, and the principle that the system should make this safe applies at every level. An eighth is review: a conflict that was managed last year may need a different arrangement this year. Finally, remember that apparently small shortcuts, such as leaving a conflict off the register because it seems minor, are how serious failures begin.

questions.prompt: A senior official has declared a conflict about a funding decision. What does proper recusal require?

options.text: Taking part in the discussion but not voting on the decision
Not taking part in the discussion or decision, not receiving the papers and not influencing others informally
Reading the papers but leaving the decision to others
Leaving the room only when the decision is formally made

questions.prompt: Why is a conflict management decision best made by someone independent of the person?

options.text: Independent people are always more senior
Independent people are obliged to approve every decision
Self-assessment is prohibited under the Code
Self-assessment risks bias and is harder to defend later

questions.prompt: What is the risk of the 'quiet conversation' after a formal recusal?

options.text: Quiet conversations are always recorded by the department and checked against the recusal
Quiet conversations are illegal under the Official Secrets Act
Quiet conversations have no effect on decisions
Informal hints or chats can circumvent the recusal and undermine the process

questions.hint: The person must stay entirely clear.

questions.prompt: Which of these can create a conflict besides money?

options.text: A common interest in a sport or hobby, which is itself enough to create a conflict
A shared train journey to work with a colleague who is involved in a related decision
Loyalty or gratitude, for example towards a former employer or mentor
A friendly greeting in a corridor from a supplier's representative whom the official has met once

questions.prompt: How might a lobbyist create a conflict risk?

options.text: By sending a published brochure about the lobbyist's sector to the officials concerned
By cultivating a relationship that later makes a decision look compromised
By attending a public consultation and asking questions in the open session like everyone else
By responding to a formal request for evidence from the department with a written submission

questions.hint: Relationships can create appearances of influence.

questions.prompt: A private office member sees what looks like an unmanaged conflict in a senior person's papers. What should they do?

options.text: Say so, through the proper route, because the system should make it safe to do so
Stay silent, since the senior person is responsible for their own declarations and papers
Raise it only if the senior person is later criticised
Remove the papers from the file so that the issue disappears and nobody is embarrassed

questions.hint: Everyone has a part to play.

questions.prompt: Why review a conflict arrangement periodically?

options.text: Circumstances change, and an arrangement that worked last year may no longer be adequate
Conflicts lapse automatically after twelve months and so must be declared again each year
Reviews are needed to satisfy the ICO, which inspects registers of interests each year
Reviews give the person a chance to renegotiate

questions.prompt: Why is leaving a minor interest off the register risky?

options.text: Minor interests are always more serious than major ones
The register is checked by the ICO, which may impose a fine for each interest left off it
Small shortcuts are how serious failures begin, and others should decide what is minor
Minor interests cannot be declared under the rules, so nobody is required to mention them

questions.hint: Do not self-select what to hide.

questions.prompt: What should a full declaration cover?

options.text: Only interests that might influence a current decision
Only financial interests above a set value
Only outside roles that are paid
Financial interests, family and close connections, past employment, outside roles and anything others might think relevant

questions.hint: Declarations should be full and honest.

questions.prompt: A senior official's close family member works for a body regulated by the official's team. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep it private, since it concerns the family member's job and not the official's own work
Declare it and agree arrangements, which may include stepping back from decisions affecting that body
Continue to work on the body's regulation but tell colleagues informally
Ask the family member to resign from the body, so that the conflict is removed entirely

items.title: L14: Hospitality, influence and the appearance of favour
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; Cabinet Office guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: At more senior levels, hospitality seldom looks like a gift. It looks like a roundtable dinner, an industry reception, a speaking invitation with travel paid, a place on a delegation or a seat at a sporting event. The question is whether accepting would reasonably appear to compromise your judgement or integrity, or give someone privileged access. Several tests help. The first is access: does accepting give the host private time with decision makers that others cannot get? Even where nothing improper is said, preferential access harms trust. The second is purpose and balance: is the event a genuine opportunity to hear a range of views or to represent the department, or is it primarily a social occasion hosted by an interested party? The third is who else is there, and who pays. An event funded by a single company with a commercial interest is different from one run by a neutral body with a transparent funding model. The fourth is transparency: entries in the register and, where the department publishes them, in published returns. The fifth is proportion: attendance as part of your role may be appropriate even where a cost is covered by the host, but extra benefits, such as accommodation upgrades or hospitality for a partner, are rarely justifiable. The sixth is repetition: a pattern of invitations from one sector may amount to influence even if each is modest. If you decline, say why and propose an alternative, such as a meeting on official premises. Leaders set the tone: if senior people take generous hospitality, junior staff will conclude that rules are flexible. A collective team token on a special occasion is different from regular gifts from one subordinate.

questions.prompt: A senior official is invited to a dinner at which a company with a commercial interest will have private time with several decision makers. Which test is most relevant?

options.text: Whether accepting would give the host preferential access that others cannot get
Whether the menu offered at the dinner is of a reasonable and modest standard
Whether the official has attended a dinner of that type before
Whether the other guests are more senior than the official

questions.prompt: Why might an event funded by a single company with a commercial interest be a concern?

options.text: Events funded by companies are always illegal
The funder may gain influence or the appearance of it, unlike a neutral body with transparent funding
Companies cannot fund events involving civil servants
The funder will always require the official to speak

questions.prompt: A host offers to pay for an upgrade in accommodation and a place for the official's partner. How should the official regard this?

options.text: As acceptable, because the host is paying for the event anyway
As acceptable if declared on the register afterwards, since the host is paying for the event anyway
Such extra benefits are rarely justifiable and should be declined
As acceptable if the official pays a small contribution

questions.prompt: A series of modest invitations arrives from one sector over six months. What is the concern?

options.text: Each invitation should be treated entirely separately
Modest invitations never need to be registered
The sector is entitled to expect equal treatment from the department on every invitation it issues
A pattern may amount to influence even if each invitation is modest

questions.prompt: What is a constructive way to decline an invitation?

options.text: Ignore the invitation altogether, since an unanswered invitation is treated as a refusal
Accept but send a junior colleague in your place, so that the department is still represented
Say that the host's company is not important enough
Explain why and propose an alternative, such as a meeting on official premises

questions.prompt: Why does it matter if leaders accept generous hospitality?

options.text: Staff may conclude that rules are flexible
Leaders are not subject to the same rules
Junior staff are not permitted to attend such events
Generosity by leaders is encouraged for morale

questions.prompt: A team gives its manager a collective token on a special occasion. How is this likely to be viewed?

options.text: As forbidden in every case, since any gift from a team to its manager breaches the rules
Differently from regular gifts from one subordinate, though policy should still be checked
As acceptable whatever its value, since it comes from colleagues and not from an outside body
As a matter for the subordinate's own conscience

questions.prompt: Which test is about whether the event offers a range of views?

options.text: Access, because privileged time with decision makers is the main concern in the rules
Proportion, because the value of the hospitality should be judged against the purpose of the visit
Purpose and balance
Repetition, because a pattern of invitations from one sector can amount to influence over time

questions.prompt: Where might an invitation be hard to justify even if no money changes hands?

options.text: Where it gives an interested party private time with decision makers that others cannot get
Where the event is held on a weekday during working hours, when the official would normally be at work
Where the event is held outside London, which makes it harder to attend and report back on it
Where the event is attended by more than one department

questions.prompt: Why is transparency in the register important at senior levels?

options.text: It exists to reward generous hosts by recording their names in a public document of record
It allows others to see and challenge patterns, and reassures the public
It is needed to calculate the pensions of the senior staff who receive the hospitality
It replaces the need for approval, since anything entered in the register is thereby authorised

items.title: L14: Impartiality in sensitive periods
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; Cabinet Office pre-election guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: Impartiality is tested most in sensitive periods, such as general elections, referendums or major political controversies. The Civil Service Code requires civil servants to serve the government of the day, whatever its political persuasion, and to keep their personal political views separate from their official work. Around elections, the Cabinet Office issues guidance, often called pre-election guidance, which asks departments to act with particular care. In general, the aim is that the Civil Service should not be used for party political purposes and should avoid actions that could influence the election outcome. That affects announcements, new commitments, use of official resources, communications and some forms of consultation. In this period civil servants should be especially careful with social media, public events and any outside activity linked to a political party. Impartiality also means being willing to serve a new government with equal commitment, and to provide advice to opposition parties during the period where permitted, according to the rules on contacts with opposition parties. A manager has a role in applying these principles. Staff should be told what is expected, questions should be answered consistently, and official resources should not be used for party business. If a politician or party representative asks you to do something that seems party political, check with the propriety or ethics team before acting. If you are asked to give advice that you think is partisan, say so politely and take advice. If a member of staff has strong personal views, remember that having views is allowed, but expressing them in a way that suggests official endorsement, or letting them colour official advice, is not. The aim is a Civil Service trusted by every party and by the public.

questions.prompt: What does the Civil Service Code require regarding political persuasion?

options.text: Supporting the party that appointed the department's leadership
Declining to work for a government that the individual did not vote for
Staying neutral by avoiding contact with any ministers
Serving the government of the day, whatever its political persuasion, with personal views kept separate from official work

questions.prompt: Why do departments take particular care around elections?

options.text: Elections suspend the application of the Code
Elections require staff to hold political opinions
The Civil Service should not be used for party political purposes or take actions that could influence the outcome
Elections are the only time impartiality matters

questions.prompt: Which of these could be affected by pre-election guidance?

options.text: Announcements, new commitments, use of official resources and some consultations
Staff holiday allocations and the arrangements for leave during the period of the election
Lunch arrangements and the use of the canteen by staff who work on election matters
The choice of stationery and the design of letterheads used for routine correspondence

questions.hint: The guidance covers activity that could influence the election.

questions.prompt: A politician's aide asks a civil servant to draft material for a party event. What should the civil servant do?

options.text: Draft it quickly, since the aide is acting for a minister
Check with the propriety or ethics team before acting
Draft it in their own time using department equipment
Ignore the request and say nothing

questions.prompt: A civil servant is asked for advice they think is partisan. What is the right approach?

options.text: Provide it, because ministers are entitled to decide for themselves what counts as partisan
Provide it, but keep a private note of disagreement
Refuse and report the minister to the press
Say so politely and take advice from the propriety team

questions.prompt: A member of staff has strong political views. What is the correct position?

options.text: Having strong views is forbidden
Views are allowed only if never spoken aloud
Having views is allowed, but expressing them as if officially endorsed or letting them colour advice is not
Views are allowed only for staff below SEO

questions.hint: The line is between views and their effect on work.

questions.prompt: What does impartiality imply about serving a new government?

options.text: Taking a few months to adjust before cooperating fully
Declining to implement policies the individual disagrees with
Serving it with equal commitment
Giving priority to the former government's commitments

questions.prompt: A manager's role during sensitive periods includes what?

options.text: Asking staff to declare how they intend to vote, so that any risk can be managed
Telling staff what is expected and answering questions consistently
Banning all use of social media for the duration of the period, whatever its purpose
Moving staff away from any political topics, so that nobody has to deal with sensitive work

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to use official resources for any party-linked activity?

options.text: It would breach impartiality and could be seen as the Civil Service supporting a party
Official resources are in short supply during elections and have to be rationed between teams
The ICO bans any use of official resources for party-linked activity during an election period
It would breach data protection law in every case

questions.hint: Resources must be used for official purposes.

questions.prompt: What is the aim of these arrangements?

options.text: A Civil Service that reflects the preferences of the current government
A Civil Service that avoids all contact with politicians
A Civil Service that is silent on policy
A Civil Service trusted by every party and by the public

questions.hint: Trust across parties is the aim.

items.title: L14: Unauthorised disclosure, authorised release and insider risk
items.source: Official Secrets Act 1989; National Security Act 2023; Government Security Classifications, legislation.gov.uk
items.body: Cases of unauthorised disclosure rarely look like spy films. They are usually a well-intentioned person, a frustrated person or a careless person, and occasionally a deliberate one. A manager should understand the spectrum. At one end is authorised release, where information is made public through a proper process: a published statistic, a decision to release under a transparency policy, an answer to a Freedom of Information request, or evidence given to a committee. At the other end is unauthorised disclosure, such as telling a journalist about a forthcoming decision, giving a document to a lobbyist, or sharing a briefing on social media. In between are grey areas: a background conversation with a stakeholder that goes further than agreed, an email forwarded to the wrong person, a presentation containing a slide that should not have been included. Insider risk describes the chance that someone with authorised access misuses it, whether deliberately or not. Factors include grievance, financial pressure, divided loyalty, ideology, coercion or simple carelessness. Most insiders are not malicious; most incidents are mistakes. Controls include need to know, access logs, clear classification, training and a culture where staff feel able to raise problems. If you suspect a colleague of unauthorised disclosure, do not investigate, confront or entrap them. Report to security, keep your suspicions confidential and let trained people deal with it. If you are the person who has made an error, report it straight away, because honesty will be taken into account. If you believe a disclosure is justified, use the whistleblowing routes, because unauthorised disclosure can be a criminal offence and you may lose protections. The National Security Act 2023 applies where the person acts to help a foreign power, and the Official Secrets Act 1989 deals with unauthorised disclosure by Crown servants of protected categories.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of authorised release?

options.text: Sending a briefing to a journalist in advance of a decision, so that coverage is accurate
Answering a Freedom of Information request through the proper process
Posting a draft policy on social media for comments
Giving a document to a lobbyist at their request

questions.hint: Authorised release uses a proper process.

questions.prompt: Which of these is most clearly unauthorised disclosure?

options.text: Publishing an official statistic on its scheduled release day, following the usual process
Giving evidence to a committee following guidance
Providing a redacted document to a requester after review
Telling a journalist about a forthcoming decision before it is announced

questions.prompt: What does insider risk describe?

options.text: The chance that someone with authorised access misuses it, deliberately or not
The risk of attack from an outside hacker
The risk of fire or flooding in a building that holds sensitive material and records
The risk that a contractor goes bankrupt and stops providing services to the department

questions.prompt: Which statement about insiders is most accurate?

options.text: Most insiders who cause incidents are working on behalf of foreign powers
Insider incidents occur only in senior grades
Most incidents are mistakes rather than malicious acts
Insiders are always motivated by money

questions.prompt: You suspect a colleague of passing documents to a journalist. What should you do?

options.text: Confront the colleague privately and ask them to explain where the documents have been going
Set a trap by leaving a marked document where only the colleague is likely to see it
Report it to security and keep your suspicions confidential
Tell the rest of the team to keep watch and report anything they notice back to you

questions.prompt: You realise you emailed a sensitive document to the wrong person. What is the best course?

options.text: Report it straight away, because honesty will be taken into account
Wait to see whether the recipient responds, since that will show whether any harm has been done
Delete the sent email from your own account and say nothing, since no copy now remains with you
Ask the recipient to keep quiet and not tell anyone

questions.prompt: Why should someone who believes a disclosure is justified use whistleblowing routes rather than leaking?

options.text: Whistleblowing routes are always quicker than a press release and result in an immediate decision
Unauthorised disclosure can be a criminal offence, and proper routes preserve legal protection
Leaking is allowed if the person is a senior official who has the authority to decide what is public
Leaks are permitted if the information is no longer classified

questions.prompt: Which factor can contribute to insider risk?

options.text: A friendly team atmosphere, which makes it easier for people to avoid reporting problems
A short commute, which gives staff more time to spend copying files after the working day
Regular training, which can draw staff's attention to the ways in which information could be misused
Grievance, financial pressure, divided loyalty or coercion

questions.prompt: Which control helps to reduce insider risk?

options.text: Giving every member of staff access to all systems so that nobody is blocked from doing the work
Removing most training so that staff are not distracted from their ordinary day-to-day work
Need to know, access logs and a culture in which staff can raise problems
Avoiding any record of who accessed what

questions.prompt: The National Security Act 2023 is most relevant where a person does what?

options.text: Forwards an email to a colleague in error
Acts to assist a foreign power
Posts about their job on social media
Fails to complete mandatory learning

items.title: L14: Handling a concern when evidence is thin
items.source: Civil Service Code; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998; ACAS guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: Managers often receive concerns that are partial, second-hand, anonymous or emotionally charged. They cannot be investigated until someone gathers the facts, yet they cannot be ignored. The first task is to listen and record what the person says, without judging. Ask open questions: what happened, when, where, who else knows, whether there is any documentary evidence. Do not promise outcomes, and do not promise confidentiality that you cannot guarantee. Explain what will happen next and when you will update them. The second task is to decide where the concern belongs. It might be a matter for line management, HR, a grievance procedure, security, a fraud team or the propriety and ethics team.  The third task is to protect people. Protect the person who raised the concern from retaliation. Protect the person it concerns from rumour and prejudgment, because they are entitled to fairness and a concern is not a finding. Keep information to those who need to know. The fourth task is to consider whether immediate steps are needed: for example, securing evidence, limiting access or changing working arrangements without implying guilt. The fifth is to avoid conducting an investigation unless it is your role, because untrained inquiries can damage evidence and fairness. The sixth is to keep records and follow up, because people who hear nothing lose trust. If the concern is about a senior person, or about your own line, take particular care to use independent routes. If evidence is lacking, the response may be to make no finding but to learn: for example, to review controls, remind staff of the rules or monitor. A properly handled concern that is not upheld still has value because it signals that the system works.

questions.prompt: A team member brings you a second-hand report of possible fraud. What is the first task?

options.text: Listen and record what they say without judging
Tell them you will deal with it personally and say nothing more
Ask them to collect proof before you do anything
Confront the person named in the report

questions.prompt: Which kind of question is most useful at the start?

options.text: Leading questions that suggest what the person should say
Questions about the person's own motives and why they have chosen to raise the concern now
Closed questions that can be answered with a simple yes or no, so the account stays short
Open questions such as what happened, when, where and who else knows

questions.prompt: Why should a manager avoid promising outcomes or absolute confidentiality?

options.text: Promises of any kind are illegal under the Code and could lead to disciplinary action
They may not be able to deliver either, and over-promising damages trust
Promises are the responsibility of HR only, and managers are not permitted to give any
Confidentiality has no value in these cases, since the matter must be shared with everyone

questions.prompt: Why is the person a concern is about owed fairness?

options.text: They are always innocent, since a concern with no evidence yet behind it should not be pursued
They must be told the identity of the person who raised it
They must be moved from the team at once, so that the concern cannot affect anyone else
A concern is not a finding, and they are entitled to a fair process

questions.prompt: Why should a manager avoid carrying out an untrained investigation?

options.text: It can damage evidence and fairness
Managers are legally forbidden to ask questions
Investigations are always done by the press office
Investigations must be done in public

questions.prompt: What step might be taken without implying guilt?

options.text: Suspending the person without explanation, so that the position is clear to the team
Announcing the concern to the team, so that everyone knows what is being looked at
Securing evidence or limiting access while the facts are established
Moving the person's desk to the middle of the office

questions.prompt: Why is follow-up important?

options.text: People who raise concerns and hear nothing lose trust
Follow-up is a legal requirement imposed by the ICO whenever a concern has been raised
Follow-up ensures that the concern is upheld, since attention to it shows it was valid
Follow-up replaces the need to investigate, since the person's account can simply be accepted

questions.prompt: Where should a manager go if the concern is about a senior person in their own line?

options.text: Raise it with the senior person first, since they are entitled to answer before anything else
Wait to see whether the senior person leaves, since the concern may then no longer matter
Use independent routes, such as the propriety team or a nominated officer
Mention it informally to colleagues to see whether they have noticed the same behaviour

questions.prompt: What might be the right response if evidence is lacking but the concern signals a weakness?

options.text: Treat the concern as malicious, since a concern without evidence is probably intended to cause trouble
Close the matter without any record, so that nothing remains on file against the person it concerned
Discipline the person who raised it, to discourage concerns that cannot be backed up with proof
Make no finding, but learn by reviewing controls or reminding staff of the rules

questions.prompt: Why does a properly handled concern that is not upheld still have value?

options.text: It shows that the person who raised the concern was mistaken and should now be given a warning
It signals that the system works and that concerns are taken seriously
It proves that the department has no problems of the kind that were raised and can close the file
It reduces the number of concerns that are likely to be raised by staff in the future

questions.hint: Trust in the system is built.

items.title: L14: Complicated probation cases
items.source: Departmental probation policies; Equality Act 2010; ACAS guidance, GOV.UK
items.body: Probation becomes complicated when it overlaps with other processes. A probationer may raise a grievance, request adjustments, become unwell, take parental leave, make a protected disclosure or complain of discrimination. Each of these changes the legal and ethical landscape. A manager should not let probation drift. Several principles apply. First, treat each issue on its merits and keep a clear record of what was raised and when, because timing can matter. If a person raises a concern and shortly afterwards faces a negative probation decision, the sequence may look like retaliation, so extra care and independent review are advisable. Second, keep processes distinct but coordinated. A grievance should be dealt with under the grievance policy, a security matter under security rules and probation under the probation policy. Take advice from HR about how to sequence them, and avoid using one to avoid another. Third, make adjustments. If a disability affects performance, ask what changes would help, trial them, and review. Do not assess against a standard that adjustments would reasonably change. Fourth, be careful with extended absence. Review dates may be adjusted. Do not penalise someone for the absence itself. Fifth, consistency: compare how you treated others in similar situations, and be ready to explain differences. Sixth, communicate honestly and in writing at key points. Seventh, take care over the final decision. It should rest on documented evidence against the agreed standards, consider alternatives such as extension or redeployment where the policy allows, be signed off at the right level and be explained to the person. Decisions made in haste or under pressure from others are the ones that fail on review. Eighth, remember wellbeing. Probation can be stressful, and the manager has a duty to act reasonably in the person's interests.

questions.prompt: A probationer raises a grievance and, shortly afterwards, the manager recommends failing them. What is the concern?

options.text: The sequence may look like retaliation, so independent review and HR advice are advisable
The grievance should automatically stop probation until the grievance has been decided in full
The recommendation is unlawful in every case, because a grievance gives complete protection
The manager is entitled to ignore the grievance when making a decision about probation

questions.prompt: Why keep processes distinct but coordinated?

options.text: Merging them makes the case simpler, quicker and cheaper for everybody who is involved in it
Probation always takes priority over a grievance
Each has its own rules and purpose, and one should not be used to avoid another
Only HR can choose which process to use, and managers have no say in how they are sequenced

questions.prompt: A disability affects a probationer's performance. What is the right approach?

options.text: Assess against the standard without any changes
Extend probation automatically
End probation early to avoid disputes
Ask what changes would help, trial them and review, without assessing against a standard that adjustments would reasonably change

questions.prompt: How should extended absence normally be handled in probation?

options.text: The absence counts against the person's objectives
Review dates may be adjusted, and the person should not be penalised for the absence itself
Probation continues unchanged regardless of the absence, so the original dates still apply in full
Probation ends automatically at the end of leave

questions.hint: Absence should not be a penalty.

questions.prompt: Why does consistency matter in probation decisions?

options.text: Consistency means every person must be treated identically regardless of facts
Different treatment of similar cases may suggest bias or unfairness, so differences should be explainable
Consistency is required only for senior staff, since junior staff are not covered by the rules
Consistency is optional in probation, since each case depends entirely on the manager's view

questions.prompt: A manager is under pressure from colleagues to fail a probationer quickly. What should they do?

options.text: Fail them to keep the team happy, since the team's views should be decisive in probation
Delay the decision indefinitely to avoid conflict, in the hope that the pressure subsides
Base the decision on documented evidence and follow the process, not on pressure
Allow the colleagues to decide, since they work most closely with the probationer each day

questions.hint: Decisions made under pressure fail on review.

questions.prompt: What alternatives to failing might a policy allow?

options.text: An extension or redeployment where the policy permits
An immediate promotion to the next grade, to reflect the effort the person has made
Anonymous transfer without explanation
An unpaid break from the post, after which probation starts again from the beginning

questions.prompt: Why is writing important at key points in probation?

options.text: It is a way to avoid speaking to the person directly, which can be uncomfortable for managers
It gives the manager legal immunity from any later claim that the process was unfair
It replaces the need for reviews, since everything important has been put in writing
It provides clear and honest communication and a record

questions.prompt: What does the manager's duty regarding wellbeing imply?

options.text: Guaranteeing the person a pass at the end of probation, whatever their performance has been
Acting reasonably in the person's interests during a stressful period
Avoiding any feedback that might upset the person while they are still settling in
Excusing underperformance entirely, since probation is intended mainly as a time of support

questions.prompt: A probationer makes a protected disclosure about a safety concern. What should the manager recognise?

options.text: That the person is protected from detriment and any negative decision needs extra care
That the disclosure ends probation automatically, because the person has raised a safety concern
That the person should be moved away from the team while the concern is examined and decided
That the disclosure should be shared with the team

items.title: L14: Hard calls in checks and offers
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard; Civil Service Recruitment Principles; Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974, GOV.UK
items.body: Edge cases in pre-employment checks test judgement and fairness. A manager should know the principles even where HR and security take the final decision. Consistency means treating like cases alike and being ready to explain differences. Proportion means that the response matches the role and the risk, not a general anxiety. Relevance means that information is considered in light of the duties of the job: a conviction for dishonesty has a different bearing on a finance role than on a role with no access to money. Honesty is central: a person who is open about a matter is usually in a stronger position than someone who conceals it, and giving false information can be a reason to withdraw an offer in itself. Data minimisation applies throughout. Fairness means offering the candidate a chance to explain, a clear account of what was found, and, where the department has an appeal or review route, information about it. The law on spent convictions under the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 generally allows people not to disclose spent convictions, though exceptions exist for certain roles, so the department must apply the correct rules. The Equality Act 2010 prevents discrimination, including in recruitment, and limits health questions before an offer. Where documents do not agree, establish the truth through fair enquiry. If a check cannot be completed, alternative evidence may be acceptable, but that is for the responsible team to decide. A manager should resist pressure to waive a check because a candidate is outstanding: the stronger the candidate, the more important it is that the process is seen to be fair. If an offer is withdrawn, the reason should be accurate and the person treated with respect.

questions.prompt: Which statement best reflects the principle of relevance in assessing a conviction?

options.text: All convictions are treated as equally serious for every role
Only convictions for violent offences matter
Convictions are irrelevant once the candidate has been shortlisted
It is considered in light of the duties of the role, so the same conviction may matter more for some roles than others

questions.prompt: Why might a candidate who is open about a matter be in a stronger position than one who conceals it?

options.text: Open candidates are automatically cleared, whatever the matter they have disclosed to the department
Concealment is always lawful
Honesty is central, and false information can itself be a reason to withdraw an offer
Openness removes the need for checks on identity, right to work and employment history

questions.prompt: What does data minimisation require in checks?

options.text: Collecting only what is needed, sharing it only with those who need it and keeping it only as long as necessary
Collecting as much as possible in case it is useful
Sharing results with the whole team
Keeping data indefinitely

questions.prompt: What does fairness to a candidate involve when a problem is found?

options.text: A decision made without any contact with the candidate, to avoid the risk of an argument
A chance to explain, a clear account of what was found and information about any review route
A decision made by the line manager alone, since they know the post and its requirements best
A decision announced to the candidate's referees first, so they can confirm it is correct

questions.prompt: What does the Rehabilitation of Offenders Act 1974 generally allow?

options.text: Employers to ask about any conviction regardless of age
People to conceal any conviction at all from the police when they are asked directly
People to delete their criminal record
People not to disclose spent convictions, with exceptions for certain roles

questions.hint: Spent convictions have limited disclosure, with exceptions.

questions.prompt: Why must the department apply the correct rules on spent convictions?

options.text: All roles are subject to the same rule, so the same conviction is always treated in the same way
Spent convictions never need to be considered, whatever the role involves and however serious they were
Exceptions depend on the role, and applying the wrong rule could be unfair or unlawful
The rules apply only to contractors

questions.prompt: Documents provided by a candidate do not agree. What is the right approach?

options.text: Establish the truth through fair enquiry
Reject the candidate immediately, since any disagreement between documents shows dishonesty
Assume that the later document is correct, since it is likely to be the most up to date
Ask other candidates for the same post for their view of which document should be believed

questions.prompt: A referee is unavailable. What might be possible?

options.text: The manager writes a reference themselves
The check is waived automatically
Alternative evidence may be acceptable, as a decision for the responsible team
The candidate is told to resubmit later with a different referee without discussion

questions.hint: Alternatives exist, decided by the right team.

questions.prompt: A manager is told a candidate is outstanding and a check should be waived to save time. What is the right response?

options.text: Agree, since outstanding candidates are low risk and the check would only delay a good appointment
Agree if the candidate offers to sign a written promise of honesty and open dealing
Agree if the manager takes personal responsibility for any problem that arises later on
Resist, because the stronger the candidate, the more important that the process is seen to be fair

questions.prompt: If an offer is withdrawn, what should be true?

options.text: The reason should be kept vague, so as to avoid a dispute with the candidate about what was found
The reason should be accurate, the process fair and the person treated with respect
The decision should be announced to the team, so they know to continue looking for a replacement
The person should not be told anything beyond the fact that the offer has been withdrawn
